title: Credibility assessment of explicit head–helmet finite element models for cranial impact protection across oblique and normal impact mechanisms under ASME V&V40
runhead: Cranial protection model credibility under V&V40
device: CIP-Alpha cranial impact protector (multi-layer helmet liner with low-friction interface)

models.name: Helmeted Head System (HHS) Model
models.what_it_computes: Whole head–helmet explicit FEA computing skull linear and angular accelerations and interface kinematics at the shell–liner–scalp interfaces

models.name: Brain Deformation (BDM) Model
models.what_it_computes: Anatomically detailed explicit FEA of cranial contents computing element-wise principal strain and strain rate fields and bulk brain rotational kinematics

mechanisms.name: Oblique rigid-anvil impact
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Represents fall or collision with tangential loading; rotational dynamics dominate and are critical for diffuse brain deformation risk

mechanisms.name: Normal compliant-anvil drop
mechanisms.why_it_matters: Represents near-normal head contact to softer surfaces; linear acceleration dominates and challenges skull load paths and liner energy management

clear_factors: Relevance of the validation activities to the COU

deviation.detail: Model risk level reported as "low-medium" with rationale

sections: Abstract
Introduction
Device under assessment: CIP-Alpha cranial impact protector
Computational models: explicit formulations and outputs (HHS and BDM)
Impact mechanisms and loading configurations
Context of Use (CoU): Pre-market design verification of skull and brain kinematics under oblique and normal impacts to support liner configuration selection and labeling claims
Model risk level and rationale: low-medium based on moderate decision consequence and decision leverage in product iteration and claim substantiation
Credibility plan grounded in ASME V&V40 and scoped factors
Numerical code verification: benchmark problems, element technology checks, and energy balance for explicit time integration
Discretization error: mesh convergence for skull kinematics and brain strain metrics per model–mechanism pair
Equivalency of input parameters: mapping of test boundary conditions, contact, friction, and material rate parameters to model inputs
Model form assessment: constitutive choices, contact formulations, and head–helmet interface representations
Relevance of validation activities to the CoU: impact severities, contact orientations, and measured observables
Software quality assurance: configuration management, solver version control, and automated regression tests
Test samples: specimens, fixtures, and headform variants
Results: credibility scoring for each factor by model–mechanism pair (HHS–oblique, HHS–normal, BDM–oblique, BDM–normal)
Discussion: implications for use in design verification and labeling claims
Limitations and future work
Conclusions
Acknowledgments
References
